q: A soil report from a prospective plot returns 20% active lime and a chlorosis index (IPC) of 60. Which rootstock decision does that force?
opts: 3309 Couderc, whose limit is nearer 11% lime
41B or Fercal, bred for high active lime
Riparia Gloire, chosen for low vigour
exp: Total limestone is not the number that matters — active (soluble) lime and the IPC (indice de pouvoir chlorosant) are, because they govern iron availability and therefore lime-induced chlorosis. 41B (Chasselas x Berlandieri) is rated to roughly 40% active lime and IPC 60, which is why it is Champagne's chalk rootstock; Fercal goes higher still (IPC ~120). 110R and 140 Ruggeri are drought specialists whose lime ceilings sit near 17-20%; 3309C is about 11%, Riparia Gloire about 6%. Match the rootstock to the limiting constraint of the site, not to its reputation.

q: Contrast isohydric and anisohydric vine behaviour under drought, and place Grenache and Syrah.
accept: isohydric closes stomata early grenache anisohydric keeps them open syrah
grenache isohydric syrah anisohydric
stomatal closure to hold water potential versus letting potential drop
conservative water use grenache risk taking water use syrah
ans: Isohydric vines close stomata early to hold leaf water potential steady — Grenache, which conserves water but shuts down photosynthesis and stalls ripening. Anisohydric vines keep stomata open and let water potential fall, ripening on but risking xylem embolism, leaf loss and sudden collapse — Syrah.
exp: This is the physiology under a lot of blending logic. Grenache tolerates hot stony sites because it rations water, but a severe deficit leaves it stuck at 15 Brix; Syrah keeps working and therefore keeps ripening, but is the first to defoliate and scorch when the reserve runs out. It is also why the same drought year reads as raisined Grenache in one plot and shrivelled, embolised Syrah in the next. The labels are a spectrum, not a switch — the same variety can shift with rootstock and soil depth.

q: Distinguish continentality from diurnal range, state how continentality is measured, and give a region at each extreme.
accept: annual swing between warmest and coldest month versus the day night swing
continentality is the annual range diurnal is the daily range
difference between hottest and coldest month means chablis continental bordeaux maritime
continentality index measures the annual temperature range diurnal is the twenty four hour swing
ans: Continentality is the annual swing — the gap between the mean temperature of the warmest and the coldest month, the figure behind the continentality (Gorczynski) index. Diurnal range is the day-night swing inside 24 hours. Strongly continental: Chablis, Ningxia, the Okanagan, much of Washington — hard winters, spring frost, a short compressed season. Strongly maritime: Bordeaux, Muscadet, Rias Baixas — mild winters, a long damp season, disease pressure rather than freeze.
exp: Candidates routinely use the two as synonyms and lose the mark. They are independent axes: Mendoza is both markedly continental and hugely diurnal, while a maritime site can still have a wide daily range if it is high and dry. The wine consequences differ too — continentality sets what survives the winter and how short the ripening window is; diurnal range sets acid retention and aromatic preservation at the end of that window.

q: Name three distinct ways a surface layer of large stones alters a vineyard's mesoclimate, and the classic case for each.
accept: store and re-radiate heat reflect light into the canopy and mulch against evaporation
heat retention at night light reflection and reduced evaporation with drainage
reradiate warmth reflect light act as a mulch
ans: They absorb daytime radiation and re-radiate it after sunset, lifting night minima in the fruit zone (the galets roules of Chateauneuf-du-Pape). They reflect and scatter light up into the underside of the canopy, so shaded fruit still colours and ripens (pale quartz and pebble sites). And they act as a mulch, cutting surface evaporation, suppressing weeds and shedding rain quickly into a free-draining profile (the Medoc's gravel croupes).
exp: Say the mechanism, not the myth. Stones do not 'ripen the grapes' — the measured effect on night minima is a degree or two, and in a heat spike the same stones cook the fruit and force growers toward taller canopies or shading. The drainage and evaporation effects are the larger and more reliable ones, which is why gravel sites shine in wet years far more obviously than warm ones.

q: Cation exchange capacity — the soil's ability to hold nutrients against leaching — is highest in:
exp: CEC comes from negatively charged surfaces holding positively charged nutrients (calcium, magnesium, potassium, ammonium). Organic matter is far and away the strongest source, followed by 2:1 swelling clays such as smectite and vermiculite; 1:1 kaolinite holds a fraction of that, and quartz sand almost nothing. The practical readings: sandy sites leach and need fertigation, so they starve in drought and flush after rain; potassium-rich clays release enough potassium to raise must pH and flatten a red's acidity, which is why potassium management on heavy soils is a wine-quality issue and not just agronomy.

q: Which kind of wind is the Zonda that sweeps Mendoza?
opts: a cold katabatic flow off the Andean icefields
a humid onshore wind that raises mildew risk
a summer monsoon that brings hail to the Uco
a dry foehn wind, warm and desiccating
exp: Classic foehn mechanics: Pacific air dumps its moisture climbing the Chilean side of the Andes, then descends and compresses on the Argentine side, arriving hot and extremely dry — humidity can fall into single figures. It blows mostly late winter into spring, so the damage is desiccation, shoot and flower injury, rather than heat stress on ripe fruit. Its other face is a benefit: a wind that dries the canopy is a wind that suppresses fungal disease, part of why Mendoza can farm organically with such ease. Do not confuse it with cold drying winds like the Mistral and Cers, or with the maritime Cape Doctor.

q: Set diurnal range aside: state roughly how fast UV radiation rises with elevation and two berry-level consequences.
accept: about ten percent more uv per thousand metres with thicker skins and more flavonols and anthocyanins
thicker skins and higher phenolics quercetin flavonols from uv
uv rises roughly ten to twelve percent per 1000 m skins thicken phenolics rise
ans: UV rises roughly 10-12% per 1,000 metres of elevation. The berry responds by thickening its skin and by accumulating UV-screening phenolics — flavonols such as quercetin, along with more anthocyanin — so high-altitude reds show deeper colour, firmer tannin and higher total phenolics than their growing-season temperature alone would predict.
exp: Altitude is two variables, not one, and candidates almost always give only the cold-night half. UV is a stress the vine answers chemically, which is why Salta and the upper Uco produce colour and grip at alcohols and temperatures that would give thin wine at sea level. It also explains the flavonol signature used in research to fingerprint high-altitude and heavily exposed fruit.

poor fruit set disorders at flowering
ans: Flowering failures: coulure (berries fail to set — 'shatter'), millerandage (mixed tiny seedless berries — 'hens and chicks')
exp: Cold, wet Junes cause both; Grenache and Merlot are prone.

q: Why does 'smoke taint' survive fermentation invisibly?
accept: glycosides release phenols later
bound volatile phenols unmasked over time
ans: Smoke phenols bind as glycosides, then hydrolyze free during fermentation/aging — taint emerges later

q: Cover crops serve vineyards by (name two):
accept: competition nitrogen erosion biodiversity structure
erosion control nitrogen fixation vigor control
ans: Erosion control, nitrogen fixing (legumes), vigor competition, soil structure and biodiversity
exp: The between-rows answer for any sustainability question.

q: Biodynamics adds what to organics, in one line?

steiner preparations celestial calendar closed farm
ans: Steiner's preparations (500–508), the celestial calendar, and the farm-as-organism ideal — Demeter certifies
exp: Horn manure (500) and horn silica (501) lead the preparations.

q: Flash détente and thermovinification are techniques for:
